claim: Microtubules consist of typically 13 protofilaments forming a tube.
source: They consist of typically 13 protofilaments forming a tube.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about microtubule structure in the Introduction.

claim: The function of microtubules depends on their ability to switch between growing and shrinking states, called dynamic instability.
source: Their function depends on their ability to switch between growing and shrinking states, called dynamic instability, which is essential for intracellular space exploration, mitosis and migration (Howard and Hyman, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Howard and Hyman, 2009.

claim: Dynamic instability is essential for intracellular space exploration, mitosis and migration.
source: Their function depends on their ability to switch between growing and shrinking states, called dynamic instability, which is essential for intracellular space exploration, mitosis and migration (Howard and Hyman, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Howard and Hyman, 2009.

claim: The dynamic properties of microtubules are tightly controlled and a target of numerous anti-cancer drugs.
source: The dynamic properties of microtubules are tightly controlled and a target of numerous anti-cancer drugs (Peterson and Mitchison, 2002; Seligmann and Twelves, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Peterson and Mitchison, 2002 and Seligmann and Twelves, 2013.

claim: The molecular mechanism of microtubule state switching is not understood.
source: However, the molecular mechanism of microtubule state switching is not understood.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the Introduction.

claim: The switch-like nature of microtubule stability is thought to depend on the existence of a stabilising GTP (or GDP-Pi) cap at the end of growing microtubules.
source: The switch-like nature of microtubule stability is thought to depend on the existence of a stabilising GTP (or GDP-Pi) cap at the end of growing microtubules as a result of addition of GTP-loaded tubulin heterodimers and subsequent GTP hydrolysis and phosphate release (Carlier, 1982; Mitchison and Kirschner, 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Carlier, 1982 and Mitchison and Kirschner, 1984.

claim: GTP cannot be visualised in individual dynamic microtubules.
source: However GTP cannot be visualised in individual dynamic microtubules; therefore the cap size and their relation to individual microtubule stability remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a technical limitation in the Introduction.

claim: The cap size and their relation to individual microtubule stability remains unknown.
source: However GTP cannot be visualised in individual dynamic microtubules; therefore the cap size and their relation to individual microtubule stability remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the Introduction.

claim: Long cap models assume several tens of tubulin layers, i.e. hundreds of nanometers long.
source: A variety of models exist, assuming either long caps (several tens of tubulin layers, i.e. hundreds of nanometers long, [Carlier et al., 1984; Chen and Hill, 1983; Mitchison and Kirschner, 1984]) or short caps (1-2 tubulin layers, i.e. 8–16 nm only, [Bayley et al., 1989; Bolterauer et al., 1999; Caplow and Shanks, 1996; Drechsel and Kirschner, 1994; Walker et al., 1991]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple papers describing long cap models.

claim: Short cap models assume 1-2 tubulin layers, i.e. 8–16 nm only.
source: A variety of models exist, assuming either long caps (several tens of tubulin layers, i.e. hundreds of nanometers long, [Carlier et al., 1984; Chen and Hill, 1983; Mitchison and Kirschner, 1984]) or short caps (1-2 tubulin layers, i.e. 8–16 nm only, [Bayley et al., 1989; Bolterauer et al., 1999; Caplow and Shanks, 1996; Drechsel and Kirschner, 1994; Walker et al., 1991]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple papers describing short cap models.

claim: Long caps would be a result of random GTP hydrolysis, causing the cap size to increase with growth speed.
source: Long caps would be a result of random GTP hydrolysis, causing the cap size to increase with growth speed.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical prediction of long cap models.

claim: Short caps would be a consequence of coupled GTP hydrolysis, which would require GTP hydrolysis to accelerate when microtubules grow faster, resulting in a short cap of constant size.
source: Short caps would be a consequence of coupled GTP hydrolysis, which would require GTP hydrolysis to accelerate when microtubules grow faster, resulting in a short cap of constant size (Bayley et al., 1989).
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical prediction of short cap models, supported by citation to Bayley et al., 1989.

claim: Proteins of the EB1 family transiently bind to growing microtubule ends as their conformation matures in a nucleotide state-dependent manner.
source: Proteins of the EB1 family (EBs) transiently bind to growing microtubule ends as their conformation matures in a nucleotide state-dependent manner (Bieling et al., 2007; Kumar and Wittmann, 2012; Maurer et al., 2011), potentially binding to the GTP (or GDP-Pi) cap (Maurer et al., 2012; Seetapun et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bieling et al., 2007; Kumar and Wittmann, 2012; Maurer et al., 2011.

claim: EBs potentially bind to the GTP (or GDP-Pi) cap.
source: Proteins of the EB1 family (EBs) transiently bind to growing microtubule ends as their conformation matures in a nucleotide state-dependent manner (Bieling et al., 2007; Kumar and Wittmann, 2012; Maurer et al., 2011), potentially binding to the GTP (or GDP-Pi) cap (Maurer et al., 2012; Seetapun et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Maurer et al., 2012; Seetapun et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2015.

claim: Before microtubules switch from growth to depolymerisation (catastrophe), the size of the EB binding region tends to decrease.
source: Before microtubules switch from growth to depolymerisation (catastrophe), the size of the EB binding region tends to decrease (Maurer et al., 2012), potentially suggesting a link between microtubule stability and the size of the EB binding region.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Maurer et al., 2012.

claim: The EB binding region extends over several hundred nanometers.
source: As this region extends over several hundred nanometers, an EB binding site cap would be a 'long cap'.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the EB binding region.

claim: Large microtubule growth fluctuations have been recently observed.
source: The recent observation of large microtubule growth fluctuations (Gardner et al., 2011a; Kerssemakers et al., 2006; Schek et al., 2007) challenged 'short cap' models because transient shrinking episodes during growth phases of up to ~ five tubulin layers (which would remove such short caps) did not cause catastrophe (Schek et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gardner et al., 2011a; Kerssemakers et al., 2006; Schek et al., 2007.

claim: Transient shrinking episodes during growth phases of up to ~ five tubulin layers did not cause catastrophe.
source: The recent observation of large microtubule growth fluctuations (Gardner et al., 2011a; Kerssemakers et al., 2006; Schek et al., 2007) challenged 'short cap' models because transient shrinking episodes during growth phases of up to ~ five tubulin layers (which would remove such short caps) did not cause catastrophe (Schek et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schek et al., 2007.

claim: Tubulin dilution causes microtubules to stop growing and prevents the addition of new capping tubulins.
source: Tubulin dilution causes microtubules to stop growing and hence prevents the addition of new capping tubulins, resulting in microtubules undergoing a catastrophe after a delay of several seconds (Walker et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Walker et al., 1991.

claim: Tubulin dilution results in microtubules undergoing a catastrophe after a delay of several seconds.
source: Tubulin dilution causes microtubules to stop growing and hence prevents the addition of new capping tubulins, resulting in microtubules undergoing a catastrophe after a delay of several seconds (Walker et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Walker et al., 1991.

claim: Delay times in tubulin dilution experiments were reported to be insensitive to the microtubule growth speed.
source: In these experiments, delay times were reported to be insensitive to the microtubule growth speed, apparently contradicting 'long cap' models that predict higher stability with increasing growth speed due to longer caps (Padinhateeri et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Padinhateeri et al., 2012.

claim: Solutions were exchanged within ~200 ms in the microfluidic device.
source: Solutions were exchanged within ~200 ms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B); the exchange itself did not affect microtubule growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C & D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The solution exchange itself did not affect microtubule growth.
source: Solutions were exchanged within ~200 ms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B); the exchange itself did not affect microtubule growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C & D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C & D.

claim: Sudden and complete removal of tubulin stopped growth, and induced a catastrophe after a delay of typically several seconds.
source: Sudden and complete removal of tubulin stopped growth, and induced a catastrophe after a delay of typically several seconds (Figure 1B, Video 1), similar to earlier observations after tubulin dilution (Walker et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Video 1, and is consistent with citation to Walker et al., 1991.

claim: Microtubule ends were tracked with a precision of ~30 nm.
source: We imaged 101 microtubules in the presence of 20 μM tubulin at 4 Hz and tracked their plus ends with a precision of ~30 nm (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the tracking methodology described and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Growth speeds varied considerably around a mean of 28 nm/s.
source: Growth speeds varied considerably around a mean of 28 nm/s (Figure 1E, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E, left.

claim: The delay times between washout and catastrophe showed a broad and non-exponential distribution, with a mean of 7.3 s.
source: The delay times between washout and catastrophe also showed a broad and non-exponential distribution, with a mean of 7.3 s (Figure 1E, right), similar to previous dilution experiments (Walker et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E, right, and is consistent with citation to Walker et al., 1991.

claim: No correlation between the delay time and the magnitude of the orientation was observed.
source: No correlation between the delay time and the magnitude of the orientation was observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, blue data), indicating that mechanical stress is not responsible for the observed variations of the momentary microtubule stabilities in our assay.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Mechanical stress is not responsible for the observed variations of the momentary microtubule stabilities in our assay.
source: No correlation between the delay time and the magnitude of the orientation was observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, blue data), indicating that mechanical stress is not responsible for the observed variations of the momentary microtubule stabilities in our assay.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of correlation between delay time and orientation.

claim: The delay times clearly increased with increasing growth speed, provided that speeds were measured directly before washout.
source: However, in contrast to a previous report (Walker et al., 1991), the delay times clearly increased with increasing growth speed, provided that speeds were measured directly before washout (Figure 2A, Figure 2B left, Spearman's rank correlation coefficient ρ = 0.69, p<10–15).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and 2B left, with statistical analysis showing strong correlation.

claim: Microtubules are more stable when they grow faster.
source: This demonstrates that microtubules are more stable when they grow faster.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the positive correlation between growth speed and delay time.

claim: The measured delay times reflect microtubule stability at the moment of tubulin washout and this stability varies over time as the growth speed fluctuates.
source: Therefore, the measured delay times reflect microtubule stability at the moment of tubulin washout and this stability varies over time as the growth speed fluctuates.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that correlation strength depends on when growth speed is measured.

claim: Microtubules shrank slowly on average at 26 nm/s before catastrophe.
source: This average track demonstrated that microtubules did not simply pause between washout and catastrophe as previous lower resolution measurements indicated (Walker et al., 1991); instead microtubules shrank slowly on average at 26 nm/s before catastrophe.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and contrasts with citation to Walker et al., 1991.

claim: Microtubules depolymerised at 480 nm/s after catastrophe.
source: This compared to a much faster depolymerisation speed of 480 nm/s after catastrophe.
evidence: This is stated as a measured value from the data.

claim: The shrinkage lengths tended to increase with growth speed.
source: These shrinkage lengths also tended to increase with growth speed (Figure 2E bottom, ρ = 0.51, p<10–7), supporting the idea that faster microtubules are more stable, apparently due to longer stabilising caps.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E bottom, with statistical analysis showing correlation.

claim: The mean shrinkage length was 220 nm, i.e. more than 25 tubulins per protofilament.
source: The mean shrinkage length was 220 nm, i.e. more than 25 tubulins per protofilament.
evidence: This is stated as a measured value from the data.

claim: The observed shrinkage length before catastrophe directly excludes models based on short stabilising caps.
source: This directly excludes models based on short stabilising caps.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the measured shrinkage length of 220 nm being much larger than short cap predictions.

claim: The observed shrinkage length before catastrophe was in the same range as previously reported 'comet lengths' of the EB binding regions in cells and in vitro.
source: Interestingly the observed shrinkage length before catastrophe was in the same range as previously reported 'comet lengths' of the EB binding regions in cells (Seetapun et al., 2012) and in vitro (Bechstedt et al., 2014; Bieling et al., 2007; Dixit et al., 2009), further supporting the possibility of a link between the EB binding region and microtubule stability, as suggested recently (Maurer et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Seetapun et al., 2012; Bechstedt et al., 2014; Bieling et al., 2007; Dixit et al., 2009; Maurer et al., 2012.

claim: After tubulin washout, the mean delay time was reduced approximately twofold to 3.5 s in the presence of 200 nM Mal3-GFP.
source: Analysis of 139 microtubules showed that after tubulin washout, the mean delay time was now reduced approximately twofold to 3.5 s (Figure 3B), despite a mild increase of the growth speed to 33 nm/s (Figure 3B, inset).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Binding of Mal3-GFP reduces the momentary microtubule stability.
source: Hence, binding of Mal3-GFP reduces the momentary microtubule stability, reminiscent of the EB-induced stimulation of catastrophes at steady state (Komarova et al., 2009; Maurer et al., 2014; Mohan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the reduced delay time in the presence of Mal3-GFP, supported by citations to Komarova et al., 2009; Maurer et al., 2014; Mohan et al., 2013.

claim: At the moment of tubulin washout the Mal3-GFP intensities at microtubule end regions varied considerably.
source: At the moment of tubulin washout the Mal3-GFP intensities at microtubule end regions varied considerably (Figure 4A, blue histogram).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The observed variation of the Mal3-GFP intensities results mainly from variations of the EB binding site numbers at different microtubule ends.
source: At a constant Mal3-GFP concentration the fraction of occupied binding sites is constant; additionally, the Mal3-GFP binding/unbinding turnover is fast compared to other processes (Bieling et al., 2007): hence, the observed variation of the Mal3-GFP intensities results mainly from variations of the EB binding site numbers at different microtubule ends (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to Bieling et al., 2007 and data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Higher Mal3-GFP intensities were observed for faster growth speeds.
source: Higher Mal3-GFP intensities were observed for faster growth speeds (ρ = 0.74, p<10–15) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B with statistical analysis showing strong correlation.

claim: Individual microtubules that happened to be growing faster at the moment of tubulin washout had longer EB site caps.
source: This indicates that individual microtubules that happened to be growing faster at the moment of tubulin washout had longer EB site caps, under otherwise identical conditions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the positive correlation between Mal3-GFP intensity and growth speed.

claim: The mean EB comet length increases with mean growth speed when varying the tubulin concentration.
source: This extends previous observations made at the ensemble level showing that the mean EB comet length increases with mean growth speed when varying the tubulin concentration (Bieling et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bieling et al., 2007.

claim: Microtubules with initially smaller EB site caps displayed shorter delay times than those with larger caps.
source: Strikingly, microtubules with initially smaller EB site caps displayed shorter delay times than those with larger caps (Figure 4C, compare top vs bottom), as demonstrated quantitatively by a strong correlation between delay times and initial Mal3-GFP end intensities (ρ = 0.78, p<10–30) (Figure 4D top, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C and 4D top with statistical analysis showing very strong correlation.

claim: At the time point of catastrophe, the total Mal3-GFP intensity was on average reduced to 29% of the initial size.
source: At the time point of catastrophe, the total Mal3-GFP intensity, and hence the size of the EB site caps, was on average reduced to 29% of the initial size (Figure 4D, compare top vs middle, considering background shown in bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Catastrophe occurs when a critical threshold of EB sites is reached.
source: The similarity of the observed reduction in size of the EB binding regions at the moment of catastrophe suggests that catastrophe occurs when a critical threshold of EB sites is reached.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the consistent reduction to 29% of initial EB sites at catastrophe.

claim: The mean Mal3-GFP intensity decay was roughly mono-exponential until catastrophe, with a measured rate of 0.33 s-1.
source: The mean Mal3-GFP intensity decay was roughly mono-exponential until catastrophe, with a measured rate of 0.33 s-1 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The measured decay rate of 0.33 s-1 could be quantitatively explained as a consequence of slow shrinkage and continued microtubule maturation after washout.
source: This rate could be quantitatively explained as a consequence of two kinetic processes removing the cap (Figure 5B): (i) slow shrinkage of the microtubule after washout (mean vs = 40 nm/s in the presence of Mal3-GFP) which removes tubulins from the end; (ii) continued microtubule maturation after washout which transforms EB binding sites everywhere in the cap into mature lattice (km = 0.16 s-1).
evidence: This is supported by kinetic modeling using measured parameters, illustrated in Figure 5B.

claim: The theoretical decay rate for the size of the EB cap is kMal3 = km(vs/vg+1) = 0.35 s-1, in good agreement with the measured value of 0.33 s-1.
source: Together with the measured mean growth speed vg = 33 nm/s before washout, these known kinetic parameter values predict a theoretical decay rate for the size of the EB cap of kMal3 = km(vs/vg+1) = 0.35 s-1 (Materials and methods), in good agreement with the measured value of 0.33 s-1.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative modeling that predicts a value close to the measured value.

claim: The good agreement between the measured and predicted delay times and shrinkage lengths shows that the temporal and spatial scale of the response of the microtubules to a sudden stop of growth can be quantitatively explained.
source: The good agreement between the measured and predicted delay times and shrinkage lengths shows that the temporal and spatial scale of the response of the microtubules to a sudden stop of growth can be quantitatively explained.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of model predictions with measured data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Average delay times extracted for seven speed groups displayed the expected positive correlation between delay times and growth speeds, showing a weaker dependence especially for the higher speed range.
source: Average delay times extracted for seven speed groups from over 200 individual microtubule tracks displayed the expected positive correlation between delay times and growth speeds, however showing a weaker dependence especially for the higher speed range (Figure 6A bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A bottom.

claim: Catastrophe is induced when a critical 'end density' of cap sites is reached in the decaying cap.
source: Together with the measured end maturation rate (Supplementary file 1A), growth and shrinkage speeds (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) for this condition, the dependence of the mean delay times on growth speed could be quantitatively explained by assuming that catastrophe is induced when a critical 'end density' of cap sites (Figure 6B, ncrit) is reached in the decaying cap.
evidence: This is supported by model fitting to the data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Catastrophe occurred when around a fifth of the initial density of cap sites (fcrit = 0.20) was left at the end of the decaying cap, i.e. ~3 per tubulin layer.
source: A fit (Figure 6A, bottom, solid red line) (Materials and methods) predicts that independent of the initial length of the stabilising cap, catastrophe occurred when around a fifth of the initial density of cap sites (fcrit = 0.20) was left at the end of the decaying cap, i.e. ~3 per tubulin layer.
evidence: This is supported by model fitting to the data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: An alternative model assuming that catastrophe occurs when a critical 'total number' of sites anywhere in the cap is reached did not agree with the data.
source: In contrast, an alternative model assuming that catastrophe occurs when a critical 'total number' of sites anywhere in the cap (Figure 6B, Ncrit) is reached did not agree with the data (Figure 6A, dashed line): this model predicts a stronger increase of delay times with growth speed for longer caps as a consequence of increasing total EB binding site numbers with cap length at washout.
evidence: This is supported by model fitting showing poor agreement with data in Figure 6A.

claim: The addition of Mal3-GFP destabilised the cap by increasing the threshold from 14% to 28% of the initial end density, i.e. from ~2 to ~4 cap sites per tubulin layer.
source: This analysis revealed furthermore that the addition of Mal3-GFP destabilised the cap by increasing the threshold from 14% to 28% of the initial end density, i.e. from ~2 to ~4 cap sites per tubulin layer (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is supported by model fitting to data shown in Figure 6C and Supplementary file 1B.

claim: Good global fits to the complete dataset were obtained for fixed end region lengths ranging between 8 and ~80 nm.
source: Good global fits to our complete dataset, consisting of all delay times and also the Mal3-GFP intensities at washout and catastrophe, were obtained for fixed end region lengths ranging between 8 and ~80 nm (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by model fitting shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: This puts an upper limit on the size of the critical part of the cap over which a minimal density needs to be maintained for microtubule stability.
source: This puts an upper limit on the size of the critical part of the cap over which a minimal density needs to be maintained for microtubule stability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the L-model fitting results.

claim: The protective cap is the EB binding region.
source: We have performed tubulin washout experiments with high spatial and temporal resolution. By simultaneously monitoring the size of the EB binding region we provide compelling evidence that the protective cap is the EB binding region.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results showing correlation between EB binding region size and microtubule stability.

claim: Faster growing microtubules have longer EB caps and are more stable after tubulin washout.
source: We found that faster growing microtubules have longer EB caps and are more stable after tubulin washout.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results showing correlations between growth speed, EB cap size, and delay time.

claim: Our results provide the first direct experimental demonstration for the original proposal that microtubule stability would increase with growth speed as a consequence of longer protective caps.
source: Therefore, our results provide the first direct experimental demonstration for the original proposal that microtubule stability would increase with growth speed as a consequence of longer protective caps (Carlier et al., 1984; Mitchison and Kirschner, 1984).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results, referencing the original proposal by Carlier et al., 1984; Mitchison and Kirschner, 1984.

claim: The protective cap is hundreds of nanometers long.
source: These observations and the increase of steady state microtubule lifetimes (Gardner et al., 2011b; Janson et al., 2003; Walker et al., 1988) with increasing growth speed as well as the recently observed shrinking episodes during steady state growth (Schek et al., 2007) are all consistent with the view that the protective cap is hundreds of nanometers long and that a random process limits its length as proposed early on for the 'random GTP hydrolysis' model (Carlier et al., 1984; Mitchison and Kirschner, 1984; Padinhateeri et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results and consistency with multiple cited studies.

claim: The momentary microtubule stability fluctuates as growth speed varies.
source: We discovered that the correlations between microtubule growth speed, EB cap length and momentary microtubule stability (delay time after tubulin removal) were lost when growth speed or EB cap size were measured several seconds before tubulin washout (Figure 2,4, Figure 4—figure supplement 2). This indicates that the momentary microtubule stability fluctuates as growth speed varies and that EB caps store a 'memory of stability' over the time scale of several seconds, probably as a consequence of the lifetimes of the EB binding sites being in this range.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results shown in Figures 2, 4, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: EB caps store a 'memory of stability' over the time scale of several seconds.
source: This indicates that the momentary microtubule stability fluctuates as growth speed varies and that EB caps store a 'memory of stability' over the time scale of several seconds, probably as a consequence of the lifetimes of the EB binding sites being in this range.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that correlation strength depends on when measurements are made relative to washout.

claim: The observation of this memory excludes memoryless models of microtubule dynamics.
source: The observation of this memory excludes memoryless models of microtubule dynamics (Bayley et al., 1989; Bolterauer et al., 1999; ).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results, with citations to memoryless models.

claim: The entire EB binding site region serves as the stabilising cap.
source: Our study shows that the entire EB binding site region serves as the stabilising cap.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: In space, the cap's stability decreases gradually with binding site density.
source: In space, its stability decreases gradually with binding site density.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results and modeling.

claim: Large parts of the cap can be lost before it loses stability.
source: Large parts of the cap can be lost before it loses stability, strictly excluding cap models where the entire cap size is small (Bayley et al., 1989; Bolterauer et al., 1999; Bowne-Anderson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results showing 29% of cap remaining at catastrophe, with citations to excluded models.

claim: The total cap is much larger than what is required for its stability.
source: The total cap is however much larger than what is required for its stability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing large cap size but catastrophe at 29% remaining.

claim: This property allows the cap to withstand strong growth fluctuations that include even short depolymerisation episodes.
source: This property allows the cap to withstand strong growth fluctuations that include even short depolymerisation episodes (Schek et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results, with citation to Schek et al., 2007.

claim: Only the highest density region of the cap, i.e. its part closest to the microtubule end, determines its stability.
source: Kinetic threshold models revealed that this behaviour can be accounted for if only the highest density region of the cap, i.e. its part closest to the microtubule end, determines its stability.
evidence: This is supported by model fitting showing better agreement for end density threshold model than total number model.

claim: For the microtubule to be stable on average 15–30% cap sites needed to be left in the end region of the cap which had a length of up to ~10 tubulin layers at most.
source: We found that for the microtubule to be stable on average 15–30% cap sites needed to be left in the end region of the cap which had a length of up to ~10 tubulin layers at most.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the L-model fitting results.

claim: EBs destabilize microtubules by acceleration of conformational end maturation.
source: Here, we gained also more mechanistic insight into how binding of EB proteins to the protective cap region influences microtubule dynamics. EBs destabilize microtubules in three ways: (i) acceleration of conformational end maturation (Maurer et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Maurer et al., 2014.

claim: EBs destabilize microtubules by acceleration of tubulin dissociation from the microtubule end.
source: (ii) acceleration of tubulin dissociation from the microtubule end (compare Figure 5A and Figure 2D), possibly due to effects of EBs on the microtubule end structure ('taper' or 'sheet') during growth (Vitre et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data in Figure 5A and Figure 2D, with citation to Vitre et al., 2008.

claim: EBs destabilize microtubules by direct structural destabilisation of the cap.
source: and (iii) direct structural destabilisation of the cap (i.e. increase of the end density threshold) (Figure 6C), which agrees with recent structural studies indicating that EBs induce strain in the microtubule lattice (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6C and citation to Zhang et al., 2015.

claim: EBs can be used to monitor the momentary stability of individual microtubules.
source: Our quantitative demonstration that the EB binding region is the protective microtubule cap means that EBs can be used to monitor the momentary stability of individual microtubules.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results showing the EB binding region is the protective cap.
